title: What is the difference between a primary key and an index — a primary key is a CONSTRAINT (uniqueness + not-null + one per table + typically the clustered index) that the DB automatically backs with an index, whereas an index is purely a performance structure (you can have many, on any columns, allowing duplicates/NULLs) that enforces no business rule?
shortTitle: What is the difference between a primary key and an index

s1_definition.profdef: A primary key is a logical constraint that declares which column or columns uniquely identify each row; it enforces uniqueness and not-null, there is at most one per table, and the database automatically backs it with an index (usually clustered). An index is purely a physical performance structure that speeds up lookups; you can create many per table on any columns, it enforces no business rule, and it may allow duplicates and nulls. In short, the primary key is a rule that happens to be implemented with an index, while an index on its own is just a shortcut with no rule attached.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, the primary key is the official rule in the banking regulations: "every account is identified by exactly one account number, it can never be blank, and no two accounts can share it." That rule is the law. An index is just a helpful finding aid the staff create to work faster, like a card catalog sorted by customer name or by branch — useful for speed, but it enforces no law, it can list the same branch many times, and you can keep several catalogs. The primary key is a promise about correctness; the index is a convenience for speed.
s1_definition.oneliner: A primary key is a correctness rule (unique, not-null, one per table) that is backed by an index; an index is a speed structure with no rule, and you can have many.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A primary key is a logical constraint that declares which column or columns uniquely identify each row; it enforces uniqueness and not-null, there is at most one per table, and the database automatically backs it with an index (usually clustered). An index is purely a physical performance structure that speeds up lookups; you can create many per table on any columns, it enforces no business rule, and it may allow duplicates and nulls. In short, the primary key is a rule that happens to be implemented with an index, while an index on its own is just a shortcut with no rule attached.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, the primary key is the official rule in the banking regulations: "every account is identified by exactly one account number, it can never be blank, and no two accounts can share it." That rule is the law. An index is just a helpful finding aid the staff create to work faster, like a card catalog sorted by customer name or by branch — useful for speed, but it enforces no law, it can list the same branch many times, and you can keep several catalogs. The primary key is a promise about correctness; the index is a convenience for speed.

**One line to remember:** A primary key is a correctness rule (unique, not-null, one per table) that is backed by an index; an index is a speed structure with no rule, and you can have many.

sections.s2_technical:
A primary key is first and foremost a constraint. It makes three guarantees: the value is unique across all rows, the value is never null, and there is exactly one primary key per table. These are business-correctness rules the database enforces so that application bugs cannot create a row with no identity or a duplicate identity. To enforce the uniqueness rule efficiently, the database automatically creates a unique index under the hood — in InnoDB and SQL Server this backing index is also the clustered index that orders the rows physically.

An index is a different kind of object entirely. Its only job is performance: it is a sorted structure that lets lookups, joins, sorts, and groupings avoid full scans. It enforces nothing about correctness unless you explicitly make it a unique index. You can create as many indexes as you like, on any columns, in any order, and a plain index happily stores duplicate values and nulls.

So the relationship is: every primary key is backed by an index, but not every index is a primary key. The primary key adds the not-null rule, the single-per-table rule, and the "this is the row's identity" semantics that foreign keys reference. An ordinary index adds none of that; it is just a shortcut.

A few practical consequences follow. Because the primary key is the row's identity, foreign keys in other tables point at it, and those relationships enforce referential integrity. Because a plain index can contain nulls and duplicates, it is suited to columns like branch code or status that repeat. And because you can have many indexes but only one primary key, index design is about choosing which query patterns to accelerate, whereas primary-key design is about choosing a stable, compact, unique identity. A senior nuance: a unique index is the middle ground — it enforces uniqueness like a primary key but allows a null (depending on the engine) and is not the row's canonical identity, which is why banks use unique indexes for secondary natural keys like PAN while keeping a compact surrogate account id as the primary key.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Every account must have one unambiguous, never-blank identity that the ledger, transactions, and foreign keys all reference. This is exactly the job of a primary key: a constraint guaranteeing uniqueness and not-null, one per table.

Problem 2 — The operations team searches accounts by branch code constantly, and branch codes repeat across thousands of accounts. This is exactly the job of a plain index: speed with duplicates allowed and no rule enforced.

Problem 3 — The PAN number is a real-world unique identifier but is not the account's canonical identity. This is exactly the middle ground of a unique index: it enforces uniqueness without being the primary key.

The mini-project defines an accounts table with a surrogate primary key, a non-unique index on branch, and a unique index on PAN, plus a transactions table whose foreign key references the primary key. The service demonstrates identity, duplicate-allowing lookup, and uniqueness enforcement.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build and run
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/pk-vs-index-service-1.0.0.jar --spring.profiles.active=dev

# PK lookup → unique, identity, FK target
psql -d bankdb -c "SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE id='SAV2001';"

# Plain index lookup → many rows, duplicates fine
psql -d bankdb -c "SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE branch_code='MUM001';"

# Unique index rejects duplicate PAN but a NULL PK is impossible
psql -d bankdb -c "INSERT INTO accounts VALUES (NULL,'X','ZZZZZ0000Z','MUM001',0);"
# Expect: ERROR — null value in column id violates not-null (PRIMARY KEY rule)
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three lookups — by account id (primary key), by branch code (plain index), and by PAN (unique index) — plus an attempt to insert a row with a null id.

Step 1 — The primary-key lookup `findById("SAV2001")` uses the constraint-backed unique clustered index. Because the key is the row's identity and is unique, it returns exactly one row and foreign keys in the transactions table point at this value.

Step 2 — The branch lookup `findByBranchCode("MUM001")` uses the plain index. It returns both Rajesh and Priya because many accounts share a branch; duplicates are expected and no rule is enforced.

Step 3 — The PAN lookup `findByPan("ABCDE1234F")` uses the unique index. It returns at most one row and would reject any attempt to insert a second account with the same PAN, yet PAN is not the account's identity — the transactions still reference the account id, not the PAN.

Step 4 — The attempt to insert a row with a null id is rejected by the primary-key constraint's not-null rule, proving the primary key enforces correctness that a plain index never would.

Step 5 — The results confirm the distinction: the primary key is a rule plus identity, the plain index is pure speed with duplicates, and the unique index is speed plus a uniqueness rule but not identity.

```text
2026-10-25 14:58:08 INFO  AccountService - PRIMARY KEY lookup SAV2001: constraint-backed identity, unique + not null
2026-10-25 14:58:08 INFO  AccountService - Plain INDEX lookup branch MUM001: duplicates allowed, no rule enforced
2026-10-25 14:58:08 INFO  AccountService - UNIQUE INDEX lookup PAN: enforces uniqueness but is NOT the identity
```

```text
  INSERT id=NULL → PRIMARY KEY not-null rule → REJECTED

```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A primary key and an index are often confused because a primary key is implemented with an index, but they are fundamentally different kinds of object. A primary key is a constraint — a business-correctness rule. It guarantees that the key column or columns are unique and never null, there is exactly one primary key per table, and that key is the row's canonical identity, which is what foreign keys in other tables reference. To enforce the uniqueness rule efficiently, the database automatically creates an index behind the primary key, and in clustered engines that backing index is also the clustered index.

An index, by itself, is purely a performance structure. Its only job is to make lookups, joins, sorts, and groupings faster by avoiding full scans. It enforces no rule unless you explicitly make it a unique index, you can create many of them on any columns, and a plain index happily stores duplicates and nulls. So every primary key is backed by an index, but most indexes are not primary keys and carry none of the identity, not-null, or one-per-table semantics.

At the National Bank of India I used all three variants in the accounts table to make the distinction concrete. The account id is the primary key — the unique, never-blank identity that the transactions table's foreign key points at. The branch code has a plain index because operations search by branch all day and thousands of accounts share a branch, so duplicates are expected and no rule applies. The PAN has a unique index because it is a real-world unique natural key, but it is not the account's identity, so transactions still reference the account id, not the PAN.

The nuance I like to close with is that the unique index is the deliberate middle ground: it enforces uniqueness just like a primary key, but it is not the row's identity and, depending on the engine, may permit a null. That is exactly why we kept a compact surrogate account id as the primary key while using a unique index for the PAN, rather than making the PAN itself the primary key.
